module.title: Unit 3: Food for Life: Quantifiers, Too & Not Enough
module.objective: Discuss meals, diet, and nutrition using quantifiers (some, any, much, many) and express excess or sufficiency with 'too' and 'not enough'.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Healthy Eating Around the World

content.summary: Welcome to the reading mission for Unit 3. In this lesson, you will read about interesting food habits around the world, learn how to talk about quantities using quantifiers like some, any, how much, and how many, and explore how to use too and not enough.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Countable and uncountable nouns, quantifiers (a/an, some, any, how much, how many, a lot of), too, and not enough.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Food items, meals, ingredients, and flavor adjectives like spicy, sweet, and healthy.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning for specific information such as quantities and ingredients, and skimming paragraphs to understand main ideas about food culture.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of short A2 texts about global food habits.
Locate specific details such as ingredients and quantities in reading passages.
Recognize and apply grammar patterns with quantifiers, too, and not enough.

contextWarmup.prompt: Which of these foods is actually a fruit, not a vegetable?
contextWarmup.explanation: The avocado is botanically a fruit because it contains seeds, even though we usually use it in savory dishes like salads.

rules: Countable nouns can be counted and have plural forms, such as an apple and two apples. Always use a or an for singular countable nouns.
Uncountable nouns cannot be counted and do not have plural forms, such as rice, water, and sugar. Never use a or an with them.
Use some in positive sentences with countable plurals and uncountable nouns, such as I have some apples and some water.
Use any in questions and negative sentences, such as Do you have any milk or I don't have any vegetables.
Use How much with uncountable nouns and How many with countable plural nouns to ask about quantities.
Use a lot of or lots of with both countable and uncountable nouns to describe large quantities.
Use too with adjectives, or too much with uncountable nouns, and too many with countable nouns to express excess.
Use not enough with nouns or not + adjective + enough to express insufficiency.

commonTrap.explanation: Learners often try to put a or an before uncountable nouns, or try to count words like water and rice.
commonTrap.wrong: Can I have a water and an apple, please?
commonTrap.correct: Can I have some water and an apple, please?

content.passageTitle: Healthy Eating Habits Around the World
paragraphs: Food is an important part of our daily lives. People around the world eat many different things to stay healthy. In some countries, breakfast is a large meal with eggs, toast, and fruit like an avocado or a banana. In other places, people prefer a simple bowl of yoghurt with fresh berries and honey. Having a good breakfast gives you enough energy for the busy morning ahead.

However, many teenagers today face problems with their daily diets. Some people eat too much fast food and do not eat enough vegetables. For example, they might have burgers and chips for lunch every day without any carrots or green salad. Doctors say we need a lot of vitamins and minerals. Eating too much sugar or salt is bad for our health. Making small changes, like adding a fresh fruit dessert or avoiding overly spicy snacks, can help everyone live a healthier life.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Picnic Quantifiers and Choices

content.summary: Focus on listening for quantifiers such as some, any, too much, and not enough in natural conversations about food and sharing. Pay attention to how speakers express amounts and dietary choices.
learningObjectives: Catch the main topic of a spoken conversation about food and sharing.
Identify details such as quantities and dietary preferences using quantifiers.
Notice how words link together in connected speech during casual conversations.

keyPhrases.note: Used with uncountable nouns when there is an excess amount.
Used to express that an amount is less than what is needed.
Used informally to mean two or a small number of items.
Used to ask for someone else's opinion or food items.

connectedSpeech.note: The auxiliary verb do reduces and links smoothly to you.
Consonant blending occurs across words without pausing.
The final t of not links directly into the vowel sound of enough.
The verb give and pronoun me combine in casual spoken English.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Food and Shopping Lists

content.summary: Practical guide on using food quantifiers, too, and not enough to write clear sentences and paragraphs in English.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Countable Nouns with Quantifiers
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + verb + a / an / some / many + countable noun
blueprintItems.example: I eat an apple and some bananas every morning.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Uncountable Nouns with Quantifiers
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + verb + some / much / a lot of + uncountable noun
blueprintItems.example: We need some rice and a lot of water for the recipe.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Expressing Excess and Insufficiency
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + verb + too + adjective / not + adjective + enough
blueprintItems.example: This soup is too hot, but the tea is not sweet enough.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize the first letter of sentences and names of specific food brands or days.
mechanicsRules.why: Sentences and proper names always start with capital letters in English.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use an apostrophe for contractions like don't or doesn't, not spaces or missing letters.
mechanicsRules.badExample: We do not have any milk, and i dont want juice.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: We do not have any milk, and I don't want juice.
mechanicsRules.why: Contractions require an apostrophe to show omitted letters.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place commas between items when writing a list of three or more foods.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I buy apples bananas and oranges at the market.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I buy apples, bananas, and oranges at the market.
mechanicsRules.why: Commas separate items in a series to make lists easy to read.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the following sentence into a negative sentence using 'any':
practicumQuestions.promptText: We have some apples in the basket.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'don't have any' instead of 'have some'.
targetAnswers: We don't have any apples in the basket.
We do not have any apples in the basket.
practicumQuestions.explanation: In negative sentences with countable plurals, change 'some' to 'any'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fill in the blank with 'much' or 'many': How _____ water do we need for the soup?
practicumQuestions.promptText: How _____ water do we need for the soup?
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'much' with uncountable nouns like water, sugar, and milk.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'too' to express excess: The tea is very hot. I cannot drink it.
practicumQuestions.promptText: The tea is very hot. I cannot drink it.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'The tea is too hot to drink.' or 'The tea is too hot.'
targetAnswers: The tea is too hot to drink.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Too' indicates an excess that prevents an action.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the capitalization and punctuation errors in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: i like eating bananas apples and oranges on sunday
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize the first word and the day of the week. Add commas between items.
targetAnswers: I like eating bananas, apples, and oranges on Sunday.
I like eating bananas apples and oranges on Sunday.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Proper nouns like days of the week, the pronoun 'I', and list commas require correct mechanics.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Transform the sentence using 'a lot of': We eat many vegetables every day.
practicumQuestions.promptText: We eat many vegetables every day.
targetAnswers: We eat a lot of vegetables every day.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'A lot of' can replace 'many' in affirmative sentences for both countable and uncountable nouns.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine these two sentences using 'and': I like chicken. I like fish.
practicumQuestions.promptText: I like chicken. I like fish.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'and' to connect the two food items.
targetAnswers: I like chicken, and I like fish.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Conjunctions like 'and' connect similar ideas or items in a sentence smoothly.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'not enough': The soup is cold. We want it warmer.
practicumQuestions.promptText: The soup is cold. We want it warmer.
targetAnswers: The soup is not hot enough.
This soup is not hot enough.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Not [adjective] enough' expresses insufficiency in a quality.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Form a question using 'How many' for this answer: There are five oranges on the table.
practicumQuestions.promptText: There are five oranges on the table.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'How many oranges are there...?'
targetAnswers: How many oranges are there on the table?
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'How many' with plural countable nouns to ask about quantity.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fix the punctuation and contraction error in the sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: she doesnt eat any meat because she is vegetarian
practicumQuestions.hint: Add an apostrophe to 'doesnt' and capitalize 'She'.
targetAnswers: She doesn't eat any meat because she is vegetarian.
She doesn't eat any meat because she is a vegetarian.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Contractions require an apostrophe, and sentences must start with a capital letter.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a complete sentence stating that you have some milk and bread in your kitchen.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'I have some milk and bread in the kitchen.'
targetAnswers: I have some milk and bread in the kitchen.
I have some milk and some bread in the kitchen.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'some' with uncountable nouns ('milk', 'bread') in affirmative sentences.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Food for Life and Quantifiers

content.summary: Master clear articulation of food vocabulary, quantifiers, and expressions with too and not enough in natural spoken English.
content.audioGuidance: Focus on sentence stress when talking about food quantities and linking words like some, any, much, and many.

pillars.name: Vowel Clarity
pillars.target: Clear short and long vowels in food words
pillars.explanation: Pronounce sounds like in carrot, yoghurt, and avocado clearly without swallowing vowels.

pillars.name: Quantifier Stress
pillars.explanation: Stress words like too, enough, much, and many to make your meaning clear.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice how main stress shifts depending on word length and syllable structure.
Two syllable food items typically have primary stress on the first syllable.
Compound nouns and longer food words place stress on specific syllables.
Descriptive adjectives and sweet course names have distinct stress patterns.
